definition: A continuous probability distribution whose curve is symmetric and bell-shaped about its mean $\mu$; $X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^{2})$ has mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$, so its standard deviation is $\sigma$.

A random variable that can take any value in an interval, such as a time or a mass; its probabilities are areas under a curve, so $\mathrm{P}(X = a) = 0$ and $\mathrm{P}(X < a) = \mathrm{P}(X \le a)$.
For a normal distribution, approximately $68\%$, $95\%$ and $99.7\%$ of values lie within $1$, $2$ and $3$ standard deviations of the mean.

Working back from a probability to a value: for a normal variable $X$ with known mean and standard deviation, finding $k$ so that $\mathrm{P}(X < k) = p$; for $\mathrm{P}(X > k) = p$, use the area $1 - p$ or set the GDC's tail to right.
